vignette: The lock turns. The concrete floor is cold beneath his bare feet. At sixty-seven, he still remembers the exact moment the heavy steel door sealed him in a windowless cell on the eastern Pacific archipelago. He is thirty-two when the ambush happens, when the zip-ties bite into his wrists and the guards drag him into the dark. For three years, he survives on rationed water, silence, and the quiet discipline of keeping his mind anchored to the architecture of the walls. He learns to read the draft that sweeps through the ventilation grate, to mark each passing week by the damp stain that creeps across the floor. When the captors finally release him, the sunlight feels like a physical weight. He does not cry. He simply stands, adjusts his coat, and walks toward the road. Back on land, he rebuilds what he can. He marries Elara, a woman who teaches him how to laugh without flinching. They share a coastal home filled with his architectural sketches and linen swatches. He opens an interior design practice, specializing in residential spaces that help families carve out routines and rest. For a while, the work functions as a kind of grounding. He reads rooms the way he once read cells—calculating sightlines, weighing the weight of light, choosing textiles that would hold a person together. Elara watches him work, her presence a steady anchor. When she dies five years ago, the house grows too large, too quiet. He keeps the practice running, but the spaces he designs begin to feel less like sanctuaries and more like stage sets. He stops inviting people in. Now, the days move differently. He wakes at three in the morning, heart hammering, convinced he hears the scrape of boots on concrete. He checks the deadbolt three times before sitting at his drafting table. When a client calls to discuss open-concept layouts, his throat tightens; the word triggers a phantom pressure against his chest, a sudden inability to breathe. He stops returning calls. He walks the same coastline route every evening, eyes fixed on the horizon, scanning for figures that are not there. His kitchen drawers hold layers of canned goods, neatly arranged but untouched. He tells himself it is practicality, but his hands tremble when he locks the door. He arranges his pencils on the desk during our sessions, each one spaced exactly half an inch apart, his breathing shallow but controlled, his gaze darting to the window whenever a siren passes outside. In session, he speaks in careful, deliberate sentences. He describes the way his body still bristles at sudden noises, how the smell of damp concrete sends him out of a café in seconds. He talks about the fatigue that settles behind his eyes, the way he watches my hands when I gesture, looking for threats or offers of help. He says he misses Elara’s voice, not just in grief, but in the quiet way she used to pull him back from the edge of his own mind. He does not ask for relief. He simply describes how he navigates the space between the lock and the open window, how he measures every room now for exits, how he continues to draw walls, even as he wonders if they are meant to keep the world out or to hold himself in.
